records.sourceFile: Collagen peptide supplementation for pain and function - Is it effective.pdf

paper.citation: Kviatkovsky SA, Hickner RC, Ormsbee MJ. Collagen peptide supplementation for pain and function: is it effective? Curr Opin Clin Nutr Metab Care. 2022;25(6):401-406.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarises recent work on collagen peptide supplementation and connective tissue turnover, pain, function, strength and body composition. It focuses on hydroxyproline-containing bioactive peptides as a possible mechanism, and concludes that the benefits may depend on those peptides.
paper.tldr: Collagen peptides may reduce pain and support strength and lean mass gains when combined with resistance training, but the human evidence is limited and mixed. The mechanism, including the role of bioactive peptides, is not yet established.
paper.methods: A narrative review of the recent literature, covering 12 to 18 months, on collagen turnover, strength and body composition, pain and function, and bioactive peptides. The review draws on mechanistic, animal and human studies, and no systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors report improved pain or function in some trials, including KOOS physical function at 10 g/day over 6 months in older adults, while a 12-week trial at 10 g/day found no difference in knee pain. In resistance training trials, collagen increased lean mass or tendon size in several studies, but strength gains were often similar to placebo, and whey protein produced greater muscle thickness gains than collagen in one 10-week trial. The authors argue that Hyp-containing bioactive peptides are the likely drivers, but this rests on animal, cell and digest studies.
paper.limitations: Narrative review with no search method. The authors' own pain and function trial is cited only from conference proceedings, and their collagen research is funded by PB Leiner, maker of the supplement used, although no conflicts are declared. The review states that the literature does not support muscle hypertrophy while also citing lean mass gains with collagen, and it notes that bioactive peptide content varies widely between products.
paper.practicalImplications: Collagen peptides are best considered as an add-on to a loading or rehabilitation program, not a replacement for it, because the reported benefits appeared alongside training. Set expectations with care: the human pain evidence is limited and mixed, and strength gains were often similar to placebo. Product composition matters, so the bioactive peptide content of a specific product should be checked before it is recommended.
paper.athleteDev: Several trials reported lean mass gains with collagen plus resistance training compared with placebo, but strength gains were often similar to placebo. Performance staff should not expect collagen to add strength beyond training alone, and whey protein gave greater muscle thickness gains in one trial.
paper.rtp: Supports collagen peptides as a possible adjunct to rehabilitation for connective tissue injury or pain, with human evidence described as limited and mixed. The review does not address return-to-sport timing, tendon loading or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Common questions and misconceptions about protein supplementation- What does the scientific evidence really show.pdf

paper.citation: Antonio J, Evans C, Ferrando AA, Stout JR, Antonio B, Cinteo H, et al. Common questions and misconceptions about protein supplementation: what does the scientific evidence really show? Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. 2024;21(1):2341903.
paper.abstract: A narrative review of 11 common questions about protein supplementation, covering kidney and bone safety, body fat, plant protein, meat, post-exercise timing, per-meal intake and endurance athletes. The authors conclude that protein is well tolerated by healthy exercise-trained people at intakes several times the RDA, and that supplements are optional rather than required.
paper.tldr: For healthy, exercise-trained people, the review finds no evidence that higher protein intakes harm the kidneys or bones, or that they add body fat on their own. Protein powder is not required, but it is a convenient way to reach daily targets.
paper.methods: The review answers 11 questions in turn, summarising selected human trials, meta-analyses, reviews and position statements. No systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality rating is described; the only search detail is a PubMed remark in the abstract.
paper.findings: The authors report intakes of 3.2 to 4.4 g/kg/day as well tolerated, and a one-year study at about 2.5 to 3.3 g/kg/day found no change in kidney markers in resistance-trained men. In one trial, 4.4 g/kg/day raised energy intake without changing body composition, and a higher-protein group had greater fat loss than a lower-protein group in another. They also state that 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day with adequate leucine and essential amino acids supports training in vegans and vegetarians, and that protein timing within an hour of training is not essential, with total daily intake more important.
paper.limitations: The narrative format with no described search or evidence grading means study selection cannot be checked, and many cited safety and body composition trials come from the lead author's own group. Several key claims rest on short or small trials and case reports, such as a two-year series of case reports in male bodybuilders cited for kidney and liver safety, and the plant protein advice is internally inconsistent (53% to 75% more plant protein in the text vs about 20% to 40% in the section summary). The lead author is CEO of the ISSN, which receives grants from protein product companies, and other authors report supplement industry funding, consulting or EAA patents.
paper.practicalImplications: For healthy, exercise-trained adults, the review treats protein intakes of up to about 4 to 5 times the RDA as tolerated, so targets can be set around training goals rather than kidney concerns. For active people, the review's 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day range is the working target, with plant-based athletes planning for more total protein to match leucine and essential amino acids. Protein powder is optional, but it is a practical way to reach a target without large calorie loads.
paper.athleteDev: The review supports 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day for athletes, with total daily protein the main driver of body composition. It suggests 20 to 30 g per meal for most people while noting that some data show larger single doses give a higher and longer anabolic response.
paper.rtp: Not an injury or return-to-sport paper. It mentions muscle damage markers after marathons and strength recovery after soccer matches, but it does not address rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Considerations for the consumption of vitamin and mineral supplements in athlete populations.pdf

paper.citation: Peeling P, Sim M, McKay AKA. Considerations for the Consumption of Vitamin and Mineral Supplements in Athlete Populations. Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: This review argues that athletes have higher micronutrient demands and that supplementation should follow a structured assessment of energy intake, diet, biochemistry, clinical status and environment. It summarises key vitamins and minerals and gives special considerations for female athletes.
paper.tldr: Assess energy intake, diet, blood markers and clinical status before adding a vitamin or mineral supplement, since food-first is the main goal. Iron, vitamin D, calcium and B vitamins have the most athlete-specific relevance, and female athletes have distinct needs.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described literature search. It draws on prior meta-analyses, trials, position statements and consensus documents on iron, B vitamins, bone health, immune function and female athlete nutrition.
paper.findings: The review cites a meta-analysis showing unchanged performance with iron supplementation in iron-deficient non-anaemic athletes, although iron supplementation improved haemoglobin and ferritin and reduced exercise fatigue in iron-deficient non-anaemic individuals. In meta-analyses of athletes and military personnel, low 25(OH)D (<30 ng/mL) was associated with greater stress fracture risk (7 studies, 3,625 participants), and vitamin D supplementation above sufficiency (>75 nmol/L) appeared to give no ergogenic benefit. Zinc (75 mg/day started within 24 hours of symptoms) reduced upper respiratory infection duration by about 33%, and vitamin C attenuated the oxidative stress and inflammatory response to a single exercise bout in 18 trials (n=313).
paper.limitations: The review has no described search method, so its evidence selection cannot be checked. Several claims are mechanistic or based on small or observational data, such as the oestrogen and iron absorption link, for which no study has directly measured iron absorption across the menstrual cycle in female athletes. A cited audit found no study that classified menstrual status to best-practice standards and only 13% of participants were female athletes. The article is based on a presentation to the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (GSSI) expert panel, and the GSSI, a division of PepsiCo, funded attendance and an honorarium for its preparation; the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
paper.practicalImplications: Before advising a supplement, assess anthropometrics, blood markers, clinical history, diet and the athlete's environment. If supplementation is chosen, plan dose, timing, food and drug interactions, duration and the frequency of biochemical monitoring, and use batch-tested products. Iron screening guidance cited in the review suggests assessing female athletes' iron status at 6-month intervals, especially when iron compromise is known.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should check energy intake and key blood markers such as iron and 25(OH)D before adding supplements to training programmes. In the cited meta-analysis, iron supplementation did not change performance in iron-deficient non-anaemic athletes.
paper.rtp: This review cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria. It mentions bone health, stress fracture and energy availability, but it gives no return-to-play protocol, and it says optimising energy intake is the primary intervention for poor bone health with low energy availability.

records.sourceFile: Contaminants in dietary supplements - Toxicity, doping risk, and current regulation.pdf

paper.citation: Zapata-Linares J, Gervasini G. Contaminants in Dietary Supplements: Toxicity, Doping Risk, and Current Regulation. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2024 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This narrative review describes undeclared contaminants found in dietary supplements, including anabolic steroids, stimulants, diuretics, selective androgen receptor modulators, growth hormone-releasing peptides and cobalt. It covers their health risks, doping implications and the current EU and US regulatory framework.
paper.tldr: Supplements used by athletes can contain undeclared steroids, stimulants, diuretics and other drugs that cause health harm and can lead to doping violations. The authors judge regulation to be weakly enforced, so athletes should take supplements with caution.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors state they conducted an exhaustive literature search for the most common contaminants, then summarized mechanism, clinical use, health risk and doping status for each. No databases, dates, selection criteria or quality appraisal are reported.
paper.findings: The authors report that anabolic-androgenic steroids and stimulants are the most frequently found contaminants, and that many designer steroids and stimulants have never been tested in humans. In cited product testing, 23 of 24 UK fitness-shop supplements contained steroids (16 of those 23 mislabeled), and 11 of 19 products sold as erythropoiesis stimulants contained cobalt and nickel, nine of them undeclared. The authors also state that good manufacturing practice certification reduces contamination risk but does not test for doping agents.
paper.limitations: A narrative review with no reported search protocol or quality appraisal, so selection and emphasis cannot be reproduced. Most contaminants are documented through product testing rather than measurement in athletes, and the authors note that the health effects of designer agents are largely untested in humans.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should advise athletes to confirm the need for any supplement with a doctor or dietitian before use, to prefer products with independent third-party testing, and to avoid online purchasing where anti-doping rules apply. The authors state that third-party testers greatly reduce contamination risk, and that good manufacturing practice certification alone does not test for doping agents.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not test performance. Its relevance to performance is that products marketed as performance or fat-burning aids can contain stimulants or steroids the athlete did not know they took, which the authors link to doping violations.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport decisions. It covers supplement contamination and doping risk, and does not address injury, rehabilitation or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Current Practice in the Measurement and Management of Vitamin D Status in Elite Sport and Parasport.pdf

paper.citation: Owens DJ, Kasper AM, Close GL. Current Practice in the Measurement and Management of Vitamin D Status in Elite Sport and Parasport. European Journal of Sport Science. 2025;25:e12305.
paper.abstract: This survey of practitioners in elite sport and parasport asked about vitamin D testing methods, supplementation decisions and information sources. Financial and logistical limits were the main barriers, venous blood was the most common sampling method, and many respondents did not know which analytical method their lab used. Supplementation decisions were usually collaborative, but criteria varied widely across practitioners.
paper.tldr: A survey of 74 elite-sport practitioners found that vitamin D testing and supplementation vary widely, and that cost and logistics limit testing. Staff who test should confirm the lab's analytical method and agree shared criteria for supplementation.
paper.methods: Practitioners in elite sport and parasport were surveyed using items validated by a Delphi panel of seven experts from 12 invited. The survey covered testing, supplementation decisions and information sources, and open-ended responses were analysed thematically.
paper.findings: Of 74 respondents, about a quarter did not test athletes' vitamin D status, and all of these reported no budget or did not know whether one existed. Among those who tested, 94% (n = 53) used venous blood, and 89.5% (n = 51) did not know the analytical method, mostly sending samples to an external lab or hospital. Supplementation was reported as a joint support-team decision (47%) or the respondent's sole decision (44%), and 97% (n = 71) used academic literature as an information source.
paper.limitations: The survey is self-reported and lab methods and test results were not verified. Recruitment was through social media and email, and the sample was skewed to UK respondents (48 of 74) and to nutritionists and dietitians (64 of 74). The results report 74 respondents but the discussion says 73, one percentage (n = , 20%) has no count, and a second breakdown of who makes the supplementation decision (club doctor 38%, combined team 30%, nutritionist 21%) does not match the 47% joint and 44% sole figures.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who test vitamin D should confirm the analytical method with their lab, because most respondents did not know it and immunoassays can misestimate 25(OH)D. The authors suggest that a single spot test does not capture seasonal change, so testing at high-risk points of the year may support more individual decisions. Clear, shared supplementation criteria are also recommended by the authors, but the survey did not test whether any criteria improve outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: The survey does not measure performance. It shows that testing timing, supplementation thresholds and doses vary widely across elite teams, and open-ended responses named poor athlete adherence and a lack of perceived benefit as barriers to supplementation.
paper.rtp: The survey does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. It describes testing and supplementation practice only.

paper.citation: Gillham SH, Cole PL, Owens DJ, Chester N, Bampouras TM, McCartney D, et al. Daily Use of a Broad-Spectrum Cannabidiol Supplement Produces Detectable Concentrations of Cannabinoids in Urine Prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency: An Effect Amplified by Exercise. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, Publish Ahead of Print, 2025.
paper.abstract: Healthy, physically active adults took a broad-spectrum CBD oil (150 mg/day, with trace CBG) or a placebo for 10 weeks, then completed a fasted 90-minute moderate-intensity exercise bout with urine and blood sampling before and after. In the CBD group (n = 31), urinary CBD, CBG, CBDV and CBD metabolites were detected after 10 weeks, and several rose further after exercise. No delta-9-THC or its metabolites were found, and the authors advise athletes to avoid broad-spectrum CBD products.
paper.tldr: Ten weeks of a broad-spectrum CBD oil produced urine levels of WADA-prohibited minor cannabinoids (CBG and CBDV) in healthy adults, and fasted moderate exercise raised several of them further. Athletes subject to testing should treat broad-spectrum CBD as an anti-doping risk.
paper.methods: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel trial with deliberately unbalanced groups. Participants took 150 mg/day of a broad-spectrum CBD oil (n = 31) or an MCT oil placebo (n = 5) for 10 weeks, then completed a fasted 90-minute cycling bout at about 55% of peak wattage. Plasma and urine cannabinoids were measured by UHPLC-MS/MS at baseline, pre-exercise and post-exercise, and only the CBD group was analysed, with repeated-measures ANOVA including sex.
paper.findings: No cannabinoids were detected at baseline. After 10 weeks, urinary CBD and its metabolites were present, and CBG and CBDV were detected in 42% and 68% of pre-exercise samples, rising to 74% and 84% after exercise. Significant time effects were reported for urinary CBD, CBG, CBDV, 6-OH-CBD and 7-OH-CBD (P = 0.006 to 0.043) but not 7-COOH-CBD (P = 0.128), with no sex effect, and delta-9-THC and its metabolites were not detected in any sample.
paper.limitations: Adherence was not monitored beyond self-report, pre-exercise concentrations varied widely, the placebo group was not analysed, and CBDV is not reported on the product's certificate of analysis. Reporting conflicts should be checked: abstract and results P values differ for CBG (0.0023 vs 0.023) and 7-OH-CBD (0.009 vs 0.010), plasma and urine CBD share the same statistic (F 4.501, P 0.043), plasma 7-OH-CBD is listed twice with different results, the reported mean urinary CBDV is lower after exercise (10 vs 26 ng/mL) despite a reported increase, and results repeatedly say 'both groups' increased although only the CBD group was analysed. The fat-release explanation was not tested, the lead author's lab was funded by a CBD manufacturer, and participants were not competing athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes subject to anti-doping testing should know that a broad-spectrum CBD product can produce urine results for WADA-prohibited minor cannabinoids, and that a fasted exercise session may raise them further. The authors recommend that athletes abstain from CBD supplements until a batch-tested isolate free of minor cannabinoids is available or WADA policy changes. CBD isolates were not tested, so this study does not show their risk.
paper.athleteDev: Performance outcomes were not measured, so the study says nothing about training or competition performance. Its relevance is to anti-doping risk when athletes use broad-spectrum CBD around training sessions.
paper.rtp: The study did not include injured people or clinical outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its relevance is limited to anti-doping risk for athletes who use broad-spectrum CBD.

records.sourceFile: Determinants of food choice in athletes - A systematic scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Pelly FE, Thurecht RL, Slater G. Determinants of Food Choice in Athletes: A Systematic Scoping Review. Sports Medicine - Open. 2022;8:77.
paper.abstract: This systematic scoping review maps the individual and interpersonal determinants of food choice in athletes aged 16 years or older. It describes the sports, methods and reported determinants of 15 studies and rates their reporting quality. Health, performance and nutritional attributes recurred across studies, and the authors call for more research, particularly in female athletes.
paper.tldr: Athletes' food choices are shaped by health and performance goals, along with competition phase, experience, sport culture and the food environment. Most of the 15 included studies were surveys or interviews, and few linked food choice to diet quality.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on the Open Science Framework. Eleven databases were searched from September to November 2020 and updated in March 2021, with reference-list checks. Two reviewers screened and extracted data. Reporting quality was rated against SRQR (qualitative) and STROBE (quantitative) items.
paper.findings: Fifteen studies published from 2001 to 2021 were included, most since 2018. Health and performance were common motives, and nutritional attributes, sensory factors, familiarity, convenience, mood and weight control also recurred. Competition season, athlete experience, sport culture, nationality and sex influenced priorities, but quantitative results were inconsistent. Only one study linked food choice to diet quality, and its competition meals generally lacked fruit and dairy and included discretionary foods.
paper.limitations: No quantitative synthesis was done, and quality appraisal is limited to reporting scores. Most studies were cross-sectional surveys or interviews in small, often single-country samples, and only one focused on female athletes. The authors note that some relevant studies with generic food-choice questions may have been missed.
paper.practicalImplications: When planning nutrition education or menus, find out which factors drive each athlete's food choices, such as health, performance, taste, convenience or weight control. Competition phase, experience level and sport culture changed priorities in the included studies, so food support may need to differ across these. The authors name the Athlete Food Choice Questionnaire as the most extensively validated tool, while noting it needs further testing in specific sports and cultures.
paper.athleteDev: Frame nutrition advice around performance and health goals, since these were the most consistent influences on athlete food choice. Adjust food planning for competition season, experience level and sport culture, which changed priorities in the included studies.
paper.rtp: The review covers food choice in healthy competing athletes and reports no injury, rehabilitation or recovery outcomes. It cannot guide nutrition during return to play. The authors list food choice through injury and illness as a topic for future research.

records.sourceFile: Dietary Supplements for Health,                        Adaptation, and Recovery in Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Rawson ES, Miles MP, Larson-Meyer DE. Dietary Supplements for Health, Adaptation, and Recovery in Athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018.
paper.abstract: This scholarly review describes dietary supplements that may help athletes train or compete more effectively through health, adaptation and recovery rather than direct performance gains. Creatine, omega-3, vitamin D, probiotics, gelatin or collagen and some anti-inflammatory products are discussed. The authors recommend creatine and probiotics for specific purposes, do not recommend HMB at present, and call for more research.
paper.tldr: The review supports creatine for recovery and adaptation to intense training, and probiotics for reducing upper respiratory infections. HMB is not recommended, and the other supplements need more research before firm advice.
paper.methods: Scholarly narrative review of human, animal and mechanistic studies for each supplement. The article does not describe a systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality rating.
paper.findings: In one cited review, 7 of 15 studies found that creatine improved markers of exercise-induced muscle damage or recovery, and 8 found no effect. Most placebo-controlled probiotic trials in athletes reported lower incidence, duration or severity of upper respiratory tract infection, while performance effects were not established. Vitamin D supplementation effects on muscle function were described as equivocal; low vitamin D status was associated with more respiratory infections, and in one trial in female naval recruits vitamin D3 plus calcium reduced stress fracture incidence by 20%.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how studies were selected, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. Many cited trials are small and differ in dose, duration and outcome, and the HMB-free acid findings have been challenged. The summary lists creatine for mTBI, although human data are limited to two open-label trials in children plus animal data. The text is an accepted manuscript with no printed volume or pages, so the year is taken from the 2018 copyright line.
paper.practicalImplications: Creatine monohydrate is the supplement the review most supports for recovery and adaptation to intense training, and for periods of extreme inactivity. Check vitamin D status before supplementing, since the authors advise against indiscriminate high doses. For omega-3, the authors suggest fatty fish over fish oil at present.
paper.athleteDev: For recovery between intense training, the review supports creatine monohydrate. Probiotics may be worth starting well before travel or competition for athletes who are prone to gastrointestinal problems.
paper.rtp: The review suggests creatine may help limit muscle loss during immobilization or recovery from injury, based on seven studies with mixed outcomes. It does not address return-to-play decisions or the criteria for returning to sport.

records.sourceFile: Dietary supplement and food contaminations and their implications for doping controls.pdf

paper.citation: Walpurgis K, Thomas A, Geyer H, Mareck U, Thevis M. Dietary Supplement and Food Contaminations and Their Implications for Doping Controls. Foods. 2020;9:1012.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarizes published evidence on food and supplement contamination or adulteration with doping agents and its implications for sports drug testing. Anabolic agents and stimulants are the substances most often found as undeclared ingredients. The authors conclude that education is the main protection for athletes, supported by better laboratory methods.
paper.tldr: Supplements, some medicines and contaminated meat have caused positive doping tests, sometimes at trace levels. Education and lists of tested low-risk products are the main protections for athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of published case reports, administration studies, surveys and doping-control statistics. The authors do not describe a systematic search. The cited analytical evidence is based on chromatographic-mass spectrometric methods.
paper.findings: Anabolic agents and stimulants were the substances most often found as undeclared contaminants or deliberate additions in supplements, with diuretics, higenamine and other classes in fewer cases. In a 2004 study, 14.8% of 634 non-hormonal supplements contained undeclared anabolic steroids, and only 0.7% of 597 products did in a later repeat study. Clenbuterol residues in meat and a contaminated ibuprofen tablet are also described as sources of positive tests, and Table 1 summarizes which confirmed sources plausibly explained adverse findings.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe a systematic search, so the case selection may not be complete. The authors note that proof of causality between an adverse finding and contaminated food or supplements is difficult to provide in most instances. Contamination rates come from a few product surveys of different eras and markets, so they do not give a current overall contamination rate.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes who need supplements should use products from low-risk sources, such as independent lists of tested products. Education on the risk of contaminated supplements, meat and medicines is the main recommended protection. Athletes should act with caution when using supplements marketed for muscle gain, fat loss or mental enhancement.
paper.athleteDev: Include education on supplement contamination in performance planning, since the review names education as the main protection. Where supplements are used, direct athletes to products from low-risk sources rather than unlisted products.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It addresses contamination and doping-control risk and does not assess injured or rehabilitating athletes.

records.sourceFile: Dietary supplements as a major cause of anti-doping rule violations.pdf

paper.citation: Lauritzen F. Dietary Supplements as a Major Cause of Anti-doping Rule Violations. Front Sports Act Living. 2022;4:868228.
paper.abstract: This study reviewed 18 years of doping controls by the Norwegian national anti-doping agency to test how often supplement use caused analytical anti-doping rule violations. Athletes claimed supplements as the source in 26% of cases, and evidence supported this in about half of those. Stimulants were the most common substance group, and most high-risk products were multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements.
paper.tldr: Supplements were a likely source in about 14% of Norwegian analytical doping violations from 2003 to 2020, mostly through stimulants in pre-workout products. Staff should treat multi-ingredient pre-workout and fat-burning products as a doping risk.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of Anti-Doping Norway test statistics and case files for 192 analytical ADRVs from 2003 to 2020. Each case was reviewed using decisions by the Prosecution and Judiciary Committees, investigator and athlete documents, product evidence and laboratory reports. Supplements were categorized by Garthe and Maughan, with multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements added as a separate category.
paper.findings: In 49 of 192 cases (26%), athletes claimed a supplement caused the finding. Evidence supported a causal link in 27 cases (14%), and the committees did not exclude a supplement in 9 more, giving an estimated 14 to 19%. Stimulants were linked to 24 of the 27 supported cases, mostly methylhexanamine, and multi-ingredient pre-workout supplements were the likely source in 20; in 15 of the 27 the label declared the prohibited substance, sometimes under another name such as geranium. Most supported cases involved men (25 of 27) and recreational athletes (17 of 27), none involved sports foods, medical supplements or natural products, and the yearly share ranged from 0 to 36% with no clear trend.
paper.limitations: Data come from one national agency, so the author states results cannot be generalized, and the study did not measure supplement use prevalence. Attribution depended on documentary judgment, and athlete intent could not be established. The abstract and results text give 16 methylhexanamine cases, but Table 2 lists 17, and only 17 sums with the other stimulants to the reported 24.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes should assume that multi-ingredient pre-workout and fat-burning products may contain a banned stimulant, and check ingredients beyond the label. Anti-doping and support staff should help athletes judge the need, risk and consequences of each supplement. Independent quality-assured products are a reasonable option, though the paper notes they reduce rather than remove the risk.
paper.athleteDev: Ask athletes which supplements they take before any performance plan starts, because pre-workout and fat-burning products were the most frequent source of supplement-linked violations. Treat a stimulant-containing product as a doping risk, not only a performance aid.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It covers the sources of prohibited substances in doping-control cases and does not address injured athletes or rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Does a broad‐spectrum cannabidiol supplement improve performance in a 10-min cycler ergometer performance test.pdf

paper.citation: Gillham SH, Starke L, Welch L, Mather E, Whitelegg T, Chester N, et al. Does a broad-spectrum cannabidiol supplement improve performance in a 10-min cycle ergometer performance-test? European Journal of Sport Science. 2024;1-8.
paper.abstract: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 22 healthy participants (11 men and 11 women) completed two 10-minute cycle ergometer trials separated by 3 weeks of daily broad-spectrum CBD (150 mg) or placebo. Mean power, heart rate, blood lactate and RPE did not differ significantly between groups, so the authors conclude that the supplement did not improve performance through changes in RPE.
paper.tldr: Three weeks of a broad-spectrum CBD oil at 150 mg/day did not change mean power or perceived exertion in a 10-minute cycling time trial, compared with placebo, in 22 recreationally active adults. The result does not support a performance benefit for this product in this test.
paper.methods: Healthy recreationally active adults (24 recruited; 22 analysed, CBD n = 10 and placebo n = 12) were matched on peak power and randomly assigned to 150 mg/day broad-spectrum CBD oil or placebo oil for 3 weeks. Two 10-minute WattBike time trials, before and after supplementation, recorded power, distance, heart rate, RPE and blood lactate. Two-way ANOVAs were used.
paper.findings: Mean power did not change significantly pre to post (time effect p = 0.77; time by group p = 0.32), and RPE showed no time by group effect (p = 0.19). Heart rate and blood lactate also showed no time by group effects. Twelve of 22 participants (54%) correctly guessed their allocation.
paper.limitations: The groups were small (10 CBD, 12 placebo) and mixed by sex without a sex analysis, and the test was a single 10-minute cycling trial, so other modes and intermittent sport cannot be assessed. Both excluded participants were in the CBD group (one illness, one non-compliance), so the analysis is per protocol. Pain and recovery were not measured, although analgesia was the basis of the hypothesis, and the manufacturer provided financial support; the product contained trace cannabinoids other than CBD (CBG, CBC, CBGA).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not expect a performance gain from this broad-spectrum CBD oil in aerobic time-trial work, since 3 weeks at 150 mg/day did not change power or RPE in this sample. The authors also advise athletes to avoid off-the-shelf CBD products, because such products can contain other cannabinoids that may affect anti-doping status.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should not expect a 10-minute cycling or similar aerobic gain from this supplement in recreational adults, since the study found no change in power or perceived exertion. The paper does not test intermittent team-sport or strength performance.
paper.rtp: The study measured performance and perceived exertion in healthy recreational adults and did not measure pain, injury or recovery after exercise. It cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or support the use of CBD for pain management after injury.

records.sourceFile: Drinking Strategies- Planned                        Drinking Versus Drinking to Thirst.pdf

paper.citation: Kenefick RW. Drinking strategies: planned drinking versus drinking to thirst. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(Suppl 1):S31-S37.
paper.abstract: Thirst is alleviated before full rehydration, so when sweat rates are high and ad libitum drinking does not replace sweat losses, cumulative body water deficits develop. Planned drinking is favoured for longer exercise, especially in heat, at high intensity or high sweat rates, and when carbohydrate intake of 1 g/min is desired, while drinking to thirst may suffice for shorter, cooler or lower-intensity exercise.
paper.tldr: Drinking to thirst is often not enough during long, hot or intense endurance exercise, because thirst eases before fluid losses are replaced. A planned drinking strategy based on individual sweat rate is the author's recommendation for those conditions, while thirst-guided drinking may be sufficient for shorter or cooler sessions.
paper.methods: Narrative review of programmed drinking and drinking to thirst during exercise, with operational definitions of each strategy. The review draws on the author's earlier review of 34 endurance dehydration studies (60 observations), ad libitum drinking studies in running and cycling, and fluid-loss predictions for 5 to 42 km runs. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: Of 60 observations from 34 endurance studies, 41 (68%) showed significantly impaired performance at 2% or greater body mass loss. In several studies, ad libitum drinking replaced only about half of sweat losses, and in 14 marathon studies it commonly led to losses above 2%. Ad libitum and programmed drinking produced similar running and cycling performance in several studies, while one 30 km cycling study favoured prescribed drinking in the heat.
paper.limitations: Most dehydration studies were laboratory-based, many ad libitum studies used low-intensity or cool conditions, and field studies often started exercise euhydrated, so the 2% threshold may not be reached until late in the event. Predicted sweat losses are conservative estimates from equations not designed for sport, and fluid-loss estimates for ultra-endurance events are hard to interpret because non-fluid mass losses occur. The author declares no conflicts, yet he received an honorarium from the Gatorade Sports Science Institute, a PepsiCo division that funded the supplement.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes doing long (over about 90 minutes to 2 hours), hard or hot sessions, or who need carbohydrate at about 1 g/min, should follow a planned drinking program tailored to their measured sweat rate. Thirst-guided drinking may be sufficient for shorter sessions below about 1 to 2 hours, lower intensity work or cool conditions, and athletes should never drink to the point of weight gain.
paper.athleteDev: Use the duration, intensity and heat thresholds to decide when endurance athletes need a planned drinking plan, and have them measure sweat rate under conditions similar to competition. The review does not show a direct performance benefit of planned drinking in every sport or setting, so frame the 2% threshold as a risk marker.
paper.rtp: This review does not address return to sport. It covers fluid intake during exercise in general and does not address injury, rehabilitation or medical clearance.

records.sourceFile: Drugs and Supplements in Athletic Injury Recovery and Performance - WADA Perspective.pdf

paper.citation: Patel DR, Ergun-Longmire B. Drugs and Supplements in Athletic Injury Recovery and Performance: WADA Perspective. In: Doral MN, et al., editors. Sports Injuries. Springer Nature Switzerland; 2025. p. 243-259.
paper.abstract: The chapter reviews the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited substances and methods, the Athlete Biological Passport, and sports nutrition guidance for performance and recovery. It concludes that only a handful of supplements have shown ergogenic effects to a variable degree, namely caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate.
paper.tldr: Of the many supplements sold to athletes, the chapter finds evidence of performance effects only for caffeine, creatine, nitrate, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate, and it describes the health risks of banned drug classes. Check the current WADA and sport-specific lists rather than rely on this summary.
paper.methods: Narrative book chapter summarising the WADA prohibited list, the Athlete Biological Passport, and nutrition and supplement guidance from ACSM, the IOC, ISSN and other bodies. No systematic search method is described, and the chapter cites sources accessed in February 2023.
paper.findings: The chapter reports that anabolic agents made up 40% of the adverse analytical findings in WADA's 2021 report, from 241,430 samples, with an overall adverse finding rate of 0.65%. It lists five supplements with evidence of performance effects: caffeine (about 2 to 6 mg/kg before exercise), creatine (about 20 g/day for 5 to 7 days, or 3 to 6 g/day without loading), nitrate from beetroot juice (about 500 ml/day), beta-alanine (4 to 6 g/day for 2 to 4 weeks, with equivocal endurance evidence) and sodium bicarbonate (about 300 mg/kg 1 to 2 hours before exercise). For most banned classes it reports weak or no ergogenic evidence, and it states that anabolic agents have not been shown to enhance endurance performance.
paper.limitations: The chapter is a narrative summary with no described search method, and its sources were accessed in early 2023 while the chapter is dated 2025. The adverse finding figures come from one WADA report, which the chapter says can include Therapeutic Use Exemption findings and is not a list of adjudicated violations. Dose and timing advice is summarised from other societies' guidance rather than tested in the chapter.
paper.practicalImplications: Check each athlete's current WADA prohibited list and sport-specific rules before recommending any drug, supplement or method, since the chapter notes restrictions such as beta-blockers in archery, shooting and golf. Where iron deficiency is suspected, test serum ferritin (below 20 micrograms per litre indicates deficiency) before supplementing, because the chapter finds no evidence of an ergogenic effect of iron in athletes without deficiency. Plan fluid replacement to keep losses under 2% of body weight, since the chapter links 2% fluid loss to impaired aerobic performance, especially in hot weather.
paper.athleteDev: Performance programmes can rest on the five supplements the chapter identifies with evidence, each with dose and timing guidance, while the chapter finds little or no evidence for most banned agents. Carbohydrate and fluid planning follow the sports nutrition guidance the chapter summarises.
paper.rtp: This chapter cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its recovery content is general protein, carbohydrate and fluid guidance, and it does not assess injury rehabilitation outcomes or any treatment given after injury.
